The scope of this guideline is to provide recommendations for studies
reporting key health and justice outcomes for discharged forensic patients
and people released from prison settings returning to the community.
Specifically, the guideline aims to provide recommendations for
standardising the way in which post discharge and release community
outcomes, including reoffending, readmissions and mortality, are defined,
measured, recorded, analysed, and reported. A standardised approach will
improve comparability between studies, settings, and samples, allowing
future meta-analytic syntheses.

In undertaking a systematic systematic review and meta-analysis of
post-discharge outcomes for forensic mental health patients, it was evident
that published studies varied enormously in approaches to outcome
reporting. In particular, the following problems were identified:

1.  Most studies provide sufficient demographic details for the main
    sample, but often fail to report the same details consistently when
    reporting on the sub-samples that might be different from the main
    cohort (e.g., patients who remained in hospital vs those who were
    eventually discharged into the community)

2.  Reoffending outcomes are often inconsistently defined, with some
    studies using reoffending and reconvictions interchangeably, for
    example.

3.  Outcomes are sometimes not defined in studies. For example, some
    authors may provide details on what is counted as “violent offending”,
    while others do not explicitly define it.

4.   There is sometimes insufficient data transparency regarding the
    sample/cohort. Information about the location of secure hospitals,
    catchment areas, and whether the sample is drawn from a previously
    established dataset is often lacking. Follow-up durations are
    inconsistently reported. This makes it difficult to calculate
    person-years at-risk and prohibits comparisons being made between
    cohorts.

5.  Post-release reoffending outcomes for people being released from prison
    settings are reported without the information required to calculate
    person-years at risk, which further prevents comparison. These outcomes
    tend to be reported as cumulative prevalence rates (with varying
    durations of observation) only.
